messages.author: d6aaa4797fb20867
messages.subject: extracting predicted scores
parts:
Hi, I am trying to figure out how to extract predicted scores for an endogenous variable in a SEM. The model structure is below.

When I try "predict(mod.fit1)" I get the predicted scores for my latent variable (a in this example), but not for the endogenous variable d (which is what I want).

I'm guessing there's some easy way to do this--can anyone help?



The model:


mod1={'

a=~b+c

d~a+e+f

' }

mod.fit1=sem(mod1, data=hops)


Thanks! -Jesse

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: extracting predicted scores
parts:
Jesse--
If this is what you want to do, then invent a factor D, such that observed variable d is an errorless indicator of D (in other words, so that D = d), and then predict() should give you what you want.  Change your d~ line to D~, and add:
D =~ d.   # assuming a 1.0 loading by default
d ~~ 0*d
Unfortunately, a will be highly indeterminate with just two indicators, but if this is what you want, then this code should get it for you.
--Ed Rigdon




Sent from my iPad

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: RE: extracting predicted scores
parts:
Jesse—

     Since d is now dependent on D, other references to “d” in lavaan syntax are references to the residual of d, after accounting for D.

     The line

d~~0*d

says that the residual variance of observed variable d (the residual covariance of d with itself) is 0.  The factor D has just 1 indicator, so you must fix this residual variance to some value.  Here you want that residual variance to be 0, so that there is no distinction between d and D.

--Ed Rigdon

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: RE: extracting predicted scores
parts:
Jesse—

(1)    Well, in some cases, that residual variance will be statistically identified, even with just a single indicator, so you might choose to estimate it.  But very commonly, with a single indicator, you must fix that residual variance to something.  If you have some information about what part of the indicator’s variance is due to the factor and what part is not, then you might fix the residual variance to be equal to that latter, unrelated part.

(2)    The factor modeling literature is not concerned about factor indeterminacy, and so the advice you would get from that source might be to go ahead.  I take factor indeterminacy seriously, and I see the difference between factor and factor scores to be a major issue.  There is no escape from this problem, unless you use more and better indicators for your factors.  I don’t know that it matters at what point in the process you replace your common factor a with factor scores.  I suspect that it does not matter.

--Ed Rigdon
